q: While reviewing the letter at the office, Zara not only identified the problem,_____ also proposed a solution.
e: The correlative pair is “not only...but also.”

q: Choose the passive form of: “Sadia is writing the article.”
o: The article is written by Sadia.
The article has being written by Sadia.
The article was being written by Sadia.
The article is being written by Sadia.
e: The present continuous passive is am/is/are being + past participle.

q: The rules _____ by every employee.
e: A modal passive is modal + be + past participle.

q: People believe that the plan is effective. Choose the impersonal passive.
o: It has believed the plan effective.
The plan is believing to be effective.
It believes that the plan is effective.
It is believed that the plan is effective.
e: The impersonal passive uses “It + be + past participle + that-clause.”

q: Someone has stolen the files. Choose the passive sentence.
e: The present perfect passive is have/has been + past participle.

q: Choose the correct passive question for “Did they approve the proposal?”
e: A past simple passive question begins with was/were and uses the past participle.

q: Choose the passive form of: “Zara has written the report.”
o: The report has been written by Zara.
The report had been written by Zara.
The report is been written by Zara.
The report has written by Zara.
e: The present perfect passive is has/have been + past participle.

q: Choose the active form of: “The notice will be written by Raza.”
o: Raza will be writing the notice.
Raza will have written the notice.
e: A future simple passive with “will be” becomes “will + base verb” in the active.

q: Choose the passive form of: “Iqra wrote the notice.”
o: The notice is written by Iqra.
The notice was written by Iqra.
The notice was writing by Iqra.
e: The past simple passive is formed with was/were + past participle.

q: In the incident described in Iqra's report at the garden, convert: The officer said,“Do not enter.”
o: The officer ordered them not to enter.
The officer ordered to not entered.
The officer said them do not enter.
The officer told that they not enter.
e: A negative reported command uses verb + object + not to-infinitive.

q: For the dialogue in Raza's notice at the office, convert: She asked me,“Where do you live?”
o: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where I did lived.
She asked where do you live.
e: A reported wh-question uses statement word order and normally backshifts the tense.

q: During Ali's session at the library on the letter, convert: The teacher said to the students,“Open your books.”
o: The teacher said the students open their books.
The teacher told that open your books.
The teacher asked the students opening books.
The teacher told the students to open their books.
e: A reported command uses tell + object + to-infinitive.

q: At the clinic, while discussing the letter, Ali said,“I am tired.” Choose the reported form.
o: Ali said that he was tired.
Ali said that Ali is tired yesterday.
Ali said that I am tired.
e: With a past reporting verb, present “am” normally backshifts to “was,” and the pronoun changes to match the speaker.

q: In the project reviewed by Ali at the library, convert: She said,“I have finished the work.”
o: She said that I had finish the work.
She said that she had finished the work.
She said that she has finished the work.
She told she finished has the work.
e: Present perfect normally backshifts to past perfect in reported speech.

q: In Sadia's science letter presented at the garden, convert: She said,“The earth moves around the sun.”
o: She said the earth moving around the sun.
She told the earth to move around the sun.
She said that the earth moves around the sun.
She said that the earth moved around the sun only then.
e: A universal truth may remain in the present tense in reported speech.

q: For the exchange recorded by Ali in the notice at the museum, convert: He asked,“Have you completed the form?”
o: He asked whether have you completed the form.
He asked whether I had completed the form.
He asked had I completed the form.
He said if I complete the form?
e: A reported yes/no question uses whether/if + statement word order.

q: For the letter discussed by Sana at the station, convert: He said,“I will call you tomorrow.”
o: He said that he will call you tomorrow.
He told that he would called me tomorrow.
He said he should call I next day.
He said that he would call me the next day.
e: “Will” backshifts to “would,” and time/pronoun references change with the reporting context.

q: At the clinic, while reviewing the notice, Hira said: I wish I _____ the answer now.
e: “Wish” about an unreal present situation takes a past form.

q: After submitting the letter at the station, Ali said: I wish I _____ more carefully before submitting the form.
e: “Wish” about a past regret takes the past perfect.

q: While working on the article at the clinic, Iqra said: If I _____ more time, I would learn another language.
e: The second conditional uses past simple for a hypothetical present or future situation.

q: During the discussion of the report at the garden, Nadia said: Were I in your position, I _____ the offer.
e: Inverted “Were I...” is equivalent to “If I were...” in a second conditional.

q: In Ali's account in the report at the clinic, complete: If they had left earlier, they _____ the train.
e: The third conditional uses past perfect + would have + past participle.

q: For Ali's event at the garden described in the project, complete: If it rains tomorrow, we _____ indoors.
e: The first conditional uses present simple in the if-clause and will + base verb in the result clause.

q: For the case discussed by Sana in the notice at the garden, complete: If she had accepted the offer, she _____ in Islamabad now.
e: This mixed conditional links a past unreal condition to a present unreal result.

q: While waiting at the garden with the letter, Raza said: It is time we _____ the meeting.
e: “It is time + subject” is normally followed by a past form with present meaning.

q: In the acknowledgement of the project completed at the garden, Omar wrote: But for your help, I _____ the task.
e: “But for” introduces an unreal past condition and takes a conditional perfect result.

q: In Raza's science exercise from the letter at the office, complete: If you heat ice, it _____.
e: The zero conditional uses present simple in both clauses for general truths.

q: Regarding Iqra's notice, I do not know _____ the office at the workshop is open today.
e: “Whether” introduces an embedded yes/no question.

q: After reading Fahad's notice at the clinic, no one understands how the error _____.
e: An embedded question uses statement word order and no question mark inside the sentence.
